title: Lab 303 - Git and GitLab - Branching, Pushing, and Merge Requests

lab_objective.description: By the end of this lab, you should be able to:
objectives: Explain why teams use branches instead of making every change directly on main.
Display local branches and identify the currently checked-out branch.
Create and switch to a feature branch.
Make changes, stage files, and create commits on a feature branch.
Push a feature branch to GitLab and configure its upstream.
Compare a feature branch with main using Git commands and GitLab.
Create, review, and merge a GitLab merge request.
Update the local main branch after a merge request is merged.
Create a second feature branch and repeat the workflow for a different change.
Safely switch branches and delete a feature branch after it has been merged.
scenario: You are a Linux Systems Administrator working on a project that is already stored in GitLab.

You must not make project changes directly on main. Instead, create a feature branch, make and commit your changes there, push the branch to GitLab, and ask a reviewer to merge the changes through a merge request.
Complete two separate feature-branch examples. Merge Example 1 before starting Example 2 so the second branch starts from the latest main branch.
Prerequisite: Complete Lab 302 or use an existing local-project repository with a main branch pushed to GitLab, a working origin remote, and README.md and reports/system-report files.

Use your actual GitLab username or namespace in the remote URL. Merge request creation and merging are performed in the GitLab web interface. If your project requires approvals, request an authorized reviewer rather than approving your own request.

If you have uncommitted changes, review and commit or safely save them before continuing. Do not discard work that you need.
Concept: A branch is a movable reference to a commit. The current branch identifies the line of development your next commit will advance.

tasks.title: Understand the Branching Workflow
steps: Review this workflow before making changes:
main is the shared baseline branch.
feature/branching-guide is an isolated branch for Example 1.
Push the feature branch to origin, then create a GitLab merge request with source feature/branching-guide and target main.
After the merge request is merged, update your local main branch before starting Example 2.
Concept: A branch lets you develop a change separately from main. A merge request asks teammates to review and integrate the branch; creating a merge request does not itself merge the code.

tasks.title: Inspect Branches and Recent Commits
steps: Observe the asterisk (*) beside the currently checked-out local branch.
Concept: Local branches and remote-tracking branches are different references. For example, main is a local branch, while origin/main records your locally known state of the remote main branch.

steps: Open your local-project project in GitLab:
Navigate to Merge Requests and choose New merge request. If GitLab offers a prompt after the branch push, you may use that prompt instead.
Set the source branch to feature/branching-guide.
Set the target branch to main.
Use the title: Add Git branching guide.

Concept: The source branch contains the proposed changes. The target branch is where those changes are intended to be integrated. A merge request is a review and collaboration workflow, not a Git commit command.

Concept: Merging integrates the reviewed branch changes into the target branch. Pulling updates your local main after the merge has been completed on GitLab.

Concept: Your local main branch does not automatically update when a merge request is merged in GitLab. Use git pull to retrieve the latest target-branch history.

completion_message: Excellent work! You have completed Lab 303 - Git and GitLab - Branching, Pushing, and Merge Requests. You created two feature branches, made and committed focused changes, pushed both branches to GitLab, compared branch changes, created and reviewed merge requests, merged changes into main, updated your local repository, and cleaned up merged branches. These are core collaboration skills used in Linux administration, infrastructure automation, and DevOps teams.
